questions.q: Which hormone class acts primarily through intracellular nuclear or cytoplasmic receptors to directly regulate gene transcription?
questions.explain: Lipophilic steroid hormones, thyroid hormones (T3/T4), calcitriol, and retinoic acid diffuse across the plasma membrane to bind intracellular receptors that act as ligand-activated transcription factors.

open.q: Name the two major lipophilic hormone classes that bind intracellular receptors to directly regulate gene transcription.

questions.q: Which heterotrimeric G-protein subunit activates adenylyl cyclase to increase intracellular cAMP?
questions.explain: Ligand binding to Gs-coupled receptors exchanges GDP for GTP on the Gs alpha subunit, which dissociates from beta-gamma and stimulates adenylyl cyclase to synthesize cAMP from ATP.

open.q: Name the G-protein alpha subunit that stimulates adenylyl cyclase to raise intracellular cAMP.

questions.q: How does cholera toxin cause profuse secretory diarrhea at the molecular level?
options: Blocks cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator channels
ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha, locking it in its active GTP-bound state
questions.explain: Cholera toxin permanently ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha, abolishing its intrinsic GTPase activity and causing persistent cAMP elevation that opens CFTR chloride channels in enterocytes.

open.q: Explain the molecular mechanism by which cholera toxin causes persistent elevation of intracellular cAMP.
accept: It ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha, inhibiting its GTPase activity and locking it in an active state

questions.q: Pertussis toxin from Bordetella pertussis increases intracellular cAMP by ADP-ribosylating and inactivating which G-protein subunit?
questions.explain: Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi alpha, locking it in its inactive GDP-bound state so it can no longer inhibit adenylyl cyclase.

open.q: Name the G-protein subunit inactivated via ADP-ribosylation by pertussis toxin.

questions.q: Activation of Gq-coupled receptors stimulates phospholipase C-beta to hydrolyze PIP2 into which two second messengers?
questions.explain: Phospholipase C-beta cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into water-soluble IP3 (which mobilizes ER calcium) and membrane-bound DAG (which activates protein kinase C).

open.q: Name the two second messengers generated by phospholipase C cleavage of PIP2 downstream of Gq receptors.

questions.q: Which signaling pathway is directly activated by the insulin receptor upon insulin binding?
options: Intrinsic receptor tyrosine kinase and IRS-1/PI3K/Akt pathway
questions.explain: The insulin receptor is a preformed tetrameric receptor tyrosine kinase (alpha2-beta2) that autophosphorylates its beta subunits and phosphorylates insulin receptor substrates (IRS) to activate PI3K/Akt and Ras/MAPK.

open.q: What type of intrinsic enzymatic activity does the beta subunit of the insulin receptor possess?

questions.q: Growth hormone, prolactin, erythropoietin, and cytokines signal primarily through receptors coupled to which non-receptor tyrosine kinase family?
questions.explain: Cytokine family receptors lack intrinsic kinase activity and associate with cytosolic Janus kinases (JAKs), which phosphorylate STAT transcription factors that dimerize and translocate to the nucleus.

open.q: Name the intracellular tyrosine kinase and transcription factor pathway used by growth hormone and prolactin receptors.

questions.q: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and nitric oxide (NO) both exert their vasodilatory effects by increasing intracellular levels of which second messenger?
questions.explain: ANP activates membrane-bound guanylyl cyclase while NO activates soluble cytosolic guanylyl cyclase; both increase cGMP, activating protein kinase G to relax vascular smooth muscle.

open.q: Name the second messenger elevated by both atrial natriuretic peptide and nitric oxide.

questions.q: Which anterior pituitary hormones share an identical alpha subunit with human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)?
questions.explain: TSH, FSH, LH, and hCG are heterodimeric glycoproteins composed of a common alpha subunit and a hormone-specific beta subunit that confers receptor specificity.

open.q: Name the three anterior pituitary glycoprotein hormones that share a common alpha subunit with hCG.
accept: Thyroid-stimulating hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and luteinizing hormone

questions.q: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), and beta-endorphin are all cleaved from which single precursor polypeptide?
questions.explain: Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) is synthesized in the anterior pituitary corticotrophs and hypothalamus and cleaved by prohormone convertases into ACTH, MSH, and beta-endorphin.

open.q: Name the common precursor polypeptide from which ACTH, MSH, and beta-endorphin are derived.

questions.q: Which enzyme in the thyroid follicular colloid catalyzes iodide oxidation, iodination of thyroglobulin tyrosine residues, and coupling of MIT and DIT?
questions.explain: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidize iodide, organify tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin into MIT and DIT, and couple them into T3 and T4.

open.q: Name the heme-containing enzyme in thyroid follicles that catalyzes iodide oxidation, organification, and iodotyrosine coupling.

questions.q: Which peripheral enzyme converts circulating thyroxine (T4) into the more biologically active triiodothyronine (T3)?
questions.explain: Peripheral 5'-deiodinase (types 1 and 2, selenium-containing enzymes) removes an outer-ring iodine from T4 to generate active T3; propylthiouracil and propranolol inhibit this conversion.

open.q: Name the selenium-dependent enzyme that converts T4 to active T3 in peripheral tissues.

questions.q: Why does severe starvation or critical illness cause 'euthyroid sick syndrome' with low serum T3 and elevated reverse T3 (rT3)?
options: Inhibition of 5'-deiodinase shifts T4 metabolism toward inner-ring 5-deiodination to inactive rT3
Thyroid peroxidase is destroyed by ketone bodies
questions.explain: Caloric deprivation and stress suppress 5'-deiodinase activity, decreasing conversion of T4 to active T3 and impairing clearance of inactive reverse T3, thereby lowering basal metabolic rate.

open.q: Which inactive thyroid hormone metabolite becomes elevated in euthyroid sick syndrome due to decreased 5'-deiodinase activity?

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of steroidogenesis by converting cholesterol into pregnenolone inside mitochondria?
questions.explain: After StAR protein transports cholesterol into the inner mitochondrial membrane, CYP11A1 (cholesterol desmolase) cleaves the side chain to yield pregnenolone.

open.q: Name the mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone in steroidogenesis.

questions.q: A newborn female presents with ambiguous genitalia, severe salt-wasting dehydration, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and elevated serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Which adrenal steroidogenic enzyme is most likely deficient?
questions.explain: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for over 90% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia cases, blocking aldosterone and cortisol synthesis (causing salt wasting and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone) while shunting precursors into adrenal androgens (virilization).

open.q: Deficiency of which enzyme is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia presenting with salt wasting and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone?

questions.q: How does 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency differ clinically from 21-hydroxylase deficiency in congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
options: It does not cause virilization in females
It causes severe hyperkalemia and salt wasting
It causes hypertension and hypokalemia due to accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone
questions.explain: In 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) accumulates; because DOC has potent mineralocorticoid activity, patients develop hypertension and hypokalemia rather than salt wasting.

open.q: Name the mineralocorticoid precursor that accumulates in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency to cause hypertension and hypokalemia.

questions.q: Which cytochrome P450 enzyme converts androgens (testosterone and androstenedione) into estrogens (estradiol and estrone)?
questions.explain: Aromatase (CYP19A1) in ovarian granulosa cells, placenta, and adipose tissue aromatizes the A-ring of androgens to synthesize estrogens.

open.q: Name the enzyme that converts testosterone and androstenedione into estradiol and estrone.

questions.q: How does parathyroid hormone (PTH) increase the synthesis of active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol)?
questions.explain: PTH stimulates transcription of CYP27B1 (1-alpha-hydroxylase) in renal proximal convoluted tubule cells, converting 25-hydroxycholecalciferol into active calcitriol.

open.q: Name the renal enzyme stimulated by parathyroid hormone to convert 25-hydroxycholecalciferol into active calcitriol.

questions.q: Which peptide hormone is co-secreted in equimolar amounts with insulin from pancreatic beta-cell secretory granules and serves as a marker of endogenous insulin production?
questions.explain: Proinsulin is cleaved inside beta-cell secretory granules into mature insulin and connecting peptide (C-peptide), allowing clinicians to distinguish endogenous hyperinsulinemia from exogenous insulin administration.

open.q: Name the peptide cleaved from proinsulin and co-secreted equimolarly with insulin by pancreatic beta cells.

questions.q: Which plasma protein is synthesized exclusively by the liver and serves as the primary determinant of plasma colloid oncotic pressure?
questions.explain: Albumin (~60% of total plasma protein) is synthesized solely by hepatocytes and generates ~75-80% of plasma colloid osmotic pressure while transporting fatty acids, bilirubin, calcium, and drugs.

open.q: Name the major hepatocyte-synthesized plasma protein responsible for maintaining plasma colloid oncotic pressure.

questions.q: Why does chronic liver failure lead to peripheral edema and ascites?
options: Decreased hepatic albumin synthesis lowers plasma oncotic pressure, while portal hypertension raises hydrostatic pressure
Excess hepatic urea production draws water into tissues
Hyperglycemia causes osmotic fluid shift into the peritoneum
questions.explain: Hypoalbuminemia reduces intravascular colloid oncotic pressure, and sinusoidal fibrosis increases portal venous hydrostatic pressure, driving fluid transudation into the peritoneal cavity and interstitium.

open.q: Which two hemodynamic/oncotic abnormalities in cirrhosis combine to cause ascites and peripheral edema?
accept: Hypoalbuminemia (low oncotic pressure) and portal hypertension
Decreased plasma oncotic pressure and portal hypertension

questions.q: Which enzyme in hepatocyte smooth endoplasmic reticulum conjugates unconjugated bilirubin with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble for biliary excretion?
questions.explain: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) transfers two glucuronate groups from UDP-glucuronic acid to bilirubin, forming water-soluble bilirubin diglucuronide.

open.q: Name the hepatic enzyme that conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid.

questions.q: What is the biochemical explanation for clay-colored (acholic) stools and dark urine in obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice?
options: Excess unconjugated bilirubin is filtered by the kidneys
Bacterial overgrowth destroys urobilinogen in the colon
Conjugated bilirubin cannot enter the intestine to form stercobilin, so it regurgitates into blood and is excreted in urine
Heme oxygenase is inhibited by gallstones
questions.explain: Biliary obstruction prevents conjugated bilirubin from reaching gut bacteria (eliminating brown stercobilin in stool) and forces water-soluble bilirubin diglucuronide into plasma for glomerular filtration into urine.

open.q: Which pigment derived from intestinal bacterial metabolism of bilirubin is absent in acholic stools during biliary obstruction?

questions.q: In alcoholic hepatitis, an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2:1 is classically observed primarily because of which biochemical factor?
options: ALT is secreted directly into bile
AST is synthesized in skeletal muscle only
Alcoholism causes pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) deficiency, which impairs ALT activity more severely than AST
questions.explain: Both AST and ALT require pyridoxal phosphate (B6), which is depleted in chronic alcoholism; ALT is more sensitive to B6 depletion, and ethanol-induced mitochondrial injury releases mitochondrial AST.

open.q: Deficiency of which vitamin cofactor contributes to the characteristic AST:ALT ratio greater than 2:1 in alcoholic liver disease?

questions.q: Which serum enzyme is predominantly localized to the biliary canalicular membrane and is markedly elevated in cholestasis alongside alkaline phosphatase?
questions.explain: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) is elevated in hepatobiliary obstruction and alcohol induction, helping confirm that an elevated alkaline phosphatase is of hepatic rather than bone origin.

open.q: Name the biliary canalicular enzyme measured alongside alkaline phosphatase to confirm a hepatobiliary source of cholestasis.

questions.q: Why is prothrombin time (PT/INR) a more sensitive marker of acute hepatic synthetic failure than serum albumin?
options: Albumin is not synthesized by the liver
Coagulation factors like Factor VII have half-lives of hours, whereas albumin has a half-life of ~20 days
Prothrombin is excreted by the kidneys
Albumin is stored in large reserves in the spleen
questions.explain: Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (especially Factor VII, half-life ~6 hours) turn over rapidly, so PT prolongs within 24 hours of acute liver necrosis, whereas albumin (half-life ~20 days) takes weeks to fall.

open.q: Why does prothrombin time prolong much earlier than serum albumin falls in acute liver failure?
accept: Clotting factors like Factor VII have much shorter half-lives than albumin
Shorter half-life of coagulation factors compared to albumin

questions.q: Which hepatic acute-phase protein binds free hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis to prevent renal iron loss and tubular toxicity?
questions.explain: Haptoglobin forms stable complexes with free hemoglobin dimers that are rapidly cleared by splenic and hepatic macrophages, causing serum haptoglobin to drop sharply during hemolysis.

open.q: Name the liver-synthesized plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin during intravascular hemolysis.

questions.q: Which hepatic copper-transporting P-type ATPase is defective in Wilson disease, impairing biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin incorporation?
questions.explain: Mutations in ATP7B prevent copper incorporation into apoceruloplasmin and biliary copper excretion, leading to copper deposition in liver, basal ganglia, and Descemet membrane (Kayser-Fleischer rings).

open.q: Name the copper-transporting ATPase defective in Wilson disease.

questions.q: Which amino acid is deaminated by renal tubular glutaminase during metabolic acidosis to generate ammonium ions (NH4+) that buffer urinary H+?
questions.explain: In chronic metabolic acidosis, proximal tubular cells upregulate glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase to cleave glutamine into alpha-ketoglutarate and two NH4+ ions, excreting acid and generating new bicarbonate.

open.q: Name the amino acid metabolized by renal glutaminase to generate ammonium ions for urinary acid excretion.

questions.q: During prolonged starvation (beyond several days), which organ contributes up to 40-50% of total systemic gluconeogenesis alongside the liver?
questions.explain: The renal cortex expresses all gluconeogenic enzymes (including glucose 6-phosphatase) and uses glutamine carbon skeletons to supply nearly half of blood glucose during prolonged fasting and acidosis.

open.q: Which extrahepatic organ expresses glucose 6-phosphatase and supplies up to half of systemic glucose during prolonged starvation?

questions.q: Which enzyme in the renal proximal tubule catalyzes the rapid reversible hydration of CO2 to carbonic acid to enable bicarbonate reabsorption?
questions.explain: Luminal (type IV) and cytosolic (type II) carbonic anhydrase in the proximal convoluted tubule catalyze CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3, driving reclamation of ~85% of filtered bicarbonate.

open.q: Name the zinc-containing enzyme in the proximal tubule required for filtered bicarbonate reabsorption.

questions.q: Which glycoprotein hormone is synthesized by renal peritubular interstitial cells in response to hypoxia to stimulate red blood cell production?
questions.explain: Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) stimulates renal peritubular interstitial fibroblasts to secrete erythropoietin (EPO), which prevents apoptosis of erythroid progenitors in bone marrow.

open.q: Name the hematopoietic glycoprotein hormone secreted by the kidney in response to tissue hypoxia.

questions.q: Why does severe renal parenchymal disease cause secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy?
options: Phosphate retention and loss of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase lower calcitriol and ionized calcium, stimulating PTH secretion
Excess renal calcitriol synthesis suppresses osteoblast activity
Uremic toxins directly destroy the parathyroid glands
Increased urinary calcium excretion causes hypercalcemia
questions.explain: Failing kidneys retain phosphate (which complexes free Ca2+) and lose 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity (lowering calcitriol and gut Ca2+ absorption), producing hypocalcemia that chronically stimulates PTH.

open.q: Loss of which renal enzyme in chronic kidney disease leads to calcitriol deficiency and hypocalcemia?

questions.q: Under resting aerobic conditions, what is the primary metabolic fuel oxidized by cardiac muscle?
questions.explain: Cardiomyocytes are packed with mitochondria and derive 60-80% of their ATP from beta-oxidation of free fatty acids under resting aerobic conditions, switching toward glucose and lactate during ischemia.

open.q: What is the primary energy substrate oxidized by the human heart under normal resting aerobic conditions?

questions.q: During acute myocardial ischemia, why does intracellular pH fall rapidly and impair cardiac contractility?
options: Accelerated TCA cycle activity produces excess carbonic acid
Oxygen deprivation halts oxidative phosphorylation and forces anaerobic glycolysis with lactate and H+ accumulation
questions.explain: Ischemia blocks mitochondrial electron transport, forcing cardiomyocytes to rely on anaerobic glycolysis and ATP hydrolysis, which accumulates lactate and protons that inhibit contractile proteins and calcium handling.

open.q: Which glycolytic end product accumulates in ischemic myocardium to lower intracellular pH?

questions.q: Which adipocyte-derived peptide hormone acts on the hypothalamus to suppress appetite and increase energy expenditure, and is deficient in rare monogenic obesity?
questions.explain: Leptin is secreted by white adipocytes in proportion to fat stores and binds hypothalamic arcuate nucleus receptors (stimulating POMC/CART and inhibiting NPY/AgRP neurons) to promote satiety.

open.q: Name the satiety hormone secreted by white adipose tissue in proportion to triglyceride stores.

questions.q: Which adipokine enhances insulin sensitivity and fatty acid oxidation via AMPK activation, and has paradoxically decreased plasma levels in obesity and type 2 diabetes?
questions.explain: Adiponectin is an anti-inflammatory, insulin-sensitizing adipokine whose secretion falls as adipocytes hypertrophy in visceral obesity.

open.q: Name the insulin-sensitizing adipokine whose circulating levels decrease in obesity and insulin resistance.

questions.q: In the visual cycle of retinal rod photoreceptors, photon absorption isomerizes 11-cis-retinal bound to opsin into which configuration?
questions.explain: Light absorption isomerizes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, inducing a conformational change in rhodopsin (metarhodopsin II) that activates the G-protein transducin.

open.q: Into which isomer is 11-cis-retinal converted upon absorbing a photon in rhodopsin?

questions.q: How does light-activated rhodopsin cause hyperpolarization of retinal rod photoreceptors?
options: Activates adenylyl cyclase to open Na+ channels
Activates transducin (Gt) and cGMP phosphodiesterase, lowering cGMP and closing cGMP-gated Na+/Ca2+ channels
questions.explain: Transducin activates cGMP phosphodiesterase (PDE), hydrolyzing cGMP to 5'-GMP; falling cGMP closes cGMP-gated cation channels, hyperpolarizing the rod cell and reducing glutamate release.

open.q: Name the G-protein in retinal photoreceptors activated by metarhodopsin II to stimulate cGMP phosphodiesterase.

questions.q: Under normal fed and overnight fasting conditions, what is the sole significant energy substrate utilized by the human brain?
questions.explain: The brain lacks significant glycogen stores and cannot oxidize fatty acids across the blood-brain barrier, relying almost exclusively on glucose (~120 g/day) until prolonged starvation induces ketolysis.

open.q: Name the primary fuel utilized by the human brain under normal physiological conditions.

questions.q: Which glucose transporter mediates insulin-independent glucose uptake across brain capillary endothelial cells (the blood-brain barrier)?
questions.explain: GLUT1 is densely expressed on blood-brain barrier endothelial cells (and erythrocytes) to ensure continuous basal glucose entry into the brain regardless of insulin levels, while neurons express high-affinity GLUT3.

open.q: Name the glucose transporter responsible for transporting glucose across the blood-brain barrier.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step in catecholamine (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) synthesis?
questions.explain: Tyrosine hydroxylase converts L-tyrosine to L-DOPA using tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), O2, and Fe2+, and is the rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine biosynthesis.

open.q: Name the rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine biosynthesis.

questions.q: Which two cofactors are required by dopamine beta-hydroxylase to convert dopamine into norepinephrine inside synaptic vesicles?
questions.explain: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is a copper-containing monooxygenase located inside catecholamine storage vesicles that requires vitamin C (ascorbate) as an electron donor.

open.q: Name the vitamin and metal cofactor required by dopamine beta-hydroxylase.

questions.q: Why is carbidopa co-administered with levodopa (L-DOPA) in the treatment of Parkinson disease?
options: Carbidopa crosses the blood-brain barrier to stimulate dopamine receptors
Carbidopa inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase without crossing the blood-brain barrier
questions.explain: Carbidopa cannot cross the blood-brain barrier and inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase, preventing premature peripheral conversion of L-DOPA to dopamine (reducing nausea/arrhythmias and increasing CNS L-DOPA delivery).

open.q: Name the peripheral enzyme inhibited by carbidopa when co-administered with L-DOPA.

questions.q: Which two enzymes are responsible for the metabolic inactivation of catecholamines into vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA)?
questions.explain: Monoamine oxidase (MAO, outer mitochondrial membrane) and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT, cytosol) sequentially deaminate and O-methylate norepinephrine/epinephrine to VMA and dopamine to HVA.

open.q: Name the two enzymes that degrade catecholamines into VMA and HVA.

questions.q: Which enzyme synthesizes acetylcholine in cholinergic nerve terminals from choline and acetyl-CoA?
questions.explain: Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline in the cytoplasm of cholinergic neurons; uptake of choline via the high-affinity choline transporter is rate-limiting.

open.q: Name the enzyme that synthesizes acetylcholine from choline and acetyl-CoA.

questions.q: How do organophosphate insecticides and nerve agents such as sarin cause cholinergic crisis?
options: Irreversibly phosphorylate the active-site serine of acetylcholinesterase
questions.explain: Organophosphates covalently phosphorylate the catalytic serine hydroxyl group of acetylcholinesterase, preventing acetylcholine breakdown at neuromuscular junctions and autonomic synapses.

open.q: Name the enzyme irreversibly inhibited by organophosphate insecticides and nerve agents.

questions.q: Which pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme converts the major excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate into the major inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA?
questions.explain: Glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) removes the alpha-carboxyl group from glutamate to form gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in inhibitory interneurons.

open.q: Name the enzyme that decarboxylates glutamate to synthesize GABA.

questions.q: How does the glutamate-glutamine cycle prevent excitotoxicity after synaptic glutamate release?
options: Astrocytes take up synaptic glutamate via EAATs and convert it via glutamine synthetase into non-neuroactive glutamine for return to neurons
Neurons oxidize glutamate directly to urea in the synaptic cleft
Glutamate diffuses freely across the blood-brain barrier into venous blood
questions.explain: Perisynaptic astrocytes clear glutamate via excitatory amino acid transporters (EAAT1/2) and convert it via ATP-dependent glutamine synthetase to inert glutamine, which shuttles back to neurons for hydrolysis by glutaminase.

open.q: Name the glial enzyme that converts cleared synaptic glutamate into non-neuroactive glutamine in astrocytes.

questions.q: Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is synthesized from which essential amino acid, and what is its major urinary breakdown product?
questions.explain: Tryptophan is hydroxylated (via BH4-dependent tryptophan hydroxylase) and decarboxylated to serotonin, which is oxidized by MAO and aldehyde dehydrogenase to urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA).

open.q: Name the urinary metabolite of serotonin measured to diagnose carcinoid syndrome.

questions.q: In the pineal gland, serotonin is converted into melatonin during darkness through sequential acetylation and methylation involving which methyl donor?
questions.explain: Serotonin is N-acetylated by serotonin N-acetyltransferase (rate-limiting, suppressed by light) and O-methylated by hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase using S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to form melatonin.

open.q: Name the universal methyl group donor required for the final step of melatonin synthesis from N-acetylserotonin.

questions.q: Histamine is synthesized in mast cells, basophils, and histaminergic neurons by the decarboxylation of histidine catalyzed by which cofactor-dependent enzyme?
questions.explain: Histidine decarboxylase requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) to remove the carboxyl group of L-histidine, generating histamine.

open.q: Name the vitamin B6-dependent enzyme that converts histidine into histamine.

questions.q: Why do peptide hormones such as insulin and glucagon circulate freely in plasma with short half-lives, whereas steroid and thyroid hormones circulate bound to carrier proteins with long half-lives?
options: Peptides are water-soluble and cleared rapidly; lipophilic hormones bind plasma proteins and have longer half-lives
Peptides are covalently attached to albumin
Steroid hormones cannot be metabolised by the liver
Thyroid hormones are stored inside red blood cells
questions.explain: Hydrophilic peptide hormones dissolve in plasma and have half-lives of minutes, whereas hydrophobic steroid and thyroid hormones bind transport globulins (CBG, SHBG, TBG) and albumin, creating a circulating reservoir with half-lives of hours to days.

open.q: Name the primary specific plasma transport protein that binds thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) in blood.

questions.q: How do phosphodiesterase inhibitors such as caffeine, theophylline, and sildenafil prolong hormonal or neurotransmitter signaling?
options: Prevent hydrolysis of cAMP or cGMP into inactive 5'-AMP or 5'-GMP
questions.explain: Phosphodiesterases terminate cyclic nucleotide signaling by cleaving the 3',5'-phosphodiester bond of cAMP and cGMP; inhibitors keep cAMP or cGMP elevated.

open.q: Name the class of enzymes inhibited by sildenafil and theophylline to prolong cyclic nucleotide signaling.

questions.q: Which hypothalamic hormone inhibits the release of both growth hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary?
questions.explain: Somatostatin (growth hormone-inhibiting hormone) acts via Gi-coupled receptors on somatotrophs and thyrotrophs to suppress GH and TSH secretion.

open.q: Name the hypothalamic peptide hormone that inhibits both growth hormone and TSH secretion.

questions.q: Prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary is under tonic inhibitory control by which hypothalamic neurotransmitter?
questions.explain: Tuberoinfundibular dopamine binds D2 (Gi-coupled) receptors on lactotrophs to tonically inhibit prolactin release; D2 antagonists (antipsychotics) cause hyperprolactinemia.

open.q: Name the hypothalamic catecholamine that tonically inhibits prolactin secretion via D2 receptors.

questions.q: How does antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) increase water reabsorption in renal collecting duct principal cells?
options: Binds V2 receptors to raise cAMP and insert aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane
Binds V1 receptors to stimulate aldosterone synthesis
Activates Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporters in the proximal tubule
Inhibits carbonic anhydrase in intercalated cells
questions.explain: ADH binds basolateral V2 receptors (Gs-coupled), activating PKA to phosphorylate and translocate intracellular aquaporin-2 vesicles into the luminal membrane.

open.q: Name the water channel inserted into the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells in response to ADH.

questions.q: Why does chronic exogenous glucocorticoid therapy cause adrenal cortical atrophy and risk of adrenal crisis if stopped abruptly?
options: Glucocorticoids directly destroy zona fasciculata cells
Negative feedback suppresses CRH and ACTH, reducing trophic stimulation and causing adrenal cortical atrophy
Exogenous steroids accelerate renal cortisol clearance
questions.explain: Sustained suppression of CRH and ACTH deprives the zona fasciculata and reticularis of trophic signaling, leading to cortical atrophy and secondary adrenal insufficiency upon sudden withdrawal.

open.q: Which anterior pituitary trophic hormone is suppressed by exogenous glucocorticoids, leading to adrenal cortical atrophy?

questions.q: Which enzyme converts testosterone into the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in prostate and external genital tissues?
questions.explain: 5-alpha-reductase uses NADPH to reduce testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which has higher affinity for the androgen receptor and drives male external genitalia differentiation and prostate growth.

open.q: Name the NADPH-dependent enzyme that reduces testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with episodic headaches, diaphoresis, palpitations, and severe paroxysmal hypertension. 24-hour urine collection shows markedly elevated metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). Which tumor is most likely?
questions.explain: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of adrenal medulla chromaffin cells that overproduces epinephrine and norepinephrine, elevating plasma/urine metanephrines and VMA.

open.q: Name the catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla diagnosed by elevated plasma or urinary metanephrines and VMA.

questions.q: How does the liver detoxify lipophilic xenobiotics and drugs in Phase I and Phase II biotransformation reactions?
options: Phase I reactions add or expose polar groups; Phase II reactions conjugate metabolites to increase water solubility
Phase I conjugates drugs with albumin; Phase II oxidises them via catalase
Phase I methylates drugs in mitochondria; Phase II stores them in bile salts
Phase I cleaves peptide bonds; Phase II decarboxylates amino acids
questions.explain: Phase I reactions (primarily smooth ER cytochrome P450 monooxygenases) add functional groups (-OH, -NH2, -SH), and Phase II transferases attach bulky polar moieties (glucuronic acid, sulfate, glutathione, glycine) to enable biliary or renal excretion.

open.q: Which superfamily of heme-containing monooxygenases in hepatic smooth endoplasmic reticulum catalyzes most Phase I drug oxidations?

questions.q: A 25-year-old man ingests 25 grams of acetaminophen (paracetamol) in an overdose and develops centrilobular hepatic necrosis. Which reactive metabolite depletes hepatic glutathione and is neutralized by N-acetylcysteine?
questions.explain: When glucuronidation and sulfation pathways saturate, CYP2E1 oxidizes acetaminophen to toxic NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and alkylates hepatocyte proteins; N-acetylcysteine replenishes cysteine for glutathione synthesis.

open.q: Name the toxic reactive metabolite of acetaminophen responsible for centrilobular hepatic necrosis in overdose.

questions.q: Which hepatic acute-phase protein transports ferric iron (Fe3+) in plasma between enterocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow erythroid precursors?
questions.explain: Transferrin binds two Fe3+ ions tightly for receptor-mediated endocytosis via transferrin receptors; its saturation increases in hemochromatosis and decreases in iron deficiency anemia.

open.q: Name the liver-synthesized plasma glycoprotein that transports ferric iron in the bloodstream.

questions.q: How does the hepatic peptide hormone hepcidin regulate systemic iron homeostasis?
options: Stimulates duodenal DMT1 expression to increase iron absorption
Enhances macrophage iron release into plasma
Converts Fe3+ to Fe2+ in the stomach
Binds and induces degradation of ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, trapping iron intracellularly
questions.explain: Hepcidin, upregulated by iron overload and IL-6 during inflammation, internalizes and degrades the iron exporter ferroportin, lowering serum iron and causing anemia of chronic disease.

open.q: Name the cellular iron exporter degraded by hepcidin to reduce intestinal iron absorption and macrophage iron release.

questions.q: Deficiency of which hepatocyte-synthesized serine protease inhibitor causes both panacinar emphysema and neonatal/adult cirrhosis due to misfolded protein accumulation in the hepatocyte ER?
questions.explain: In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ), polymerized mutant A1AT accumulates as PAS-positive globules in hepatocyte ER (causing cirrhosis), while unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar walls (causing emphysema).

open.q: Name the liver-synthesized protease inhibitor whose deficiency causes both panacinar emphysema and PAS-positive hepatic globules.

questions.q: Which renal enzyme cleaves circulating angiotensinogen to angiotensin I in response to decreased renal perfusion pressure, low macula densa NaCl delivery, or beta-1 sympathetic stimulation?
questions.explain: Renin is an aspartyl protease secreted by juxtaglomerular granular cells that catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).

open.q: Name the aspartyl protease secreted by renal juxtaglomerular cells that converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.

questions.q: How does aldosterone stimulate sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in renal cortical collecting duct principal cells?
options: Binds mineralocorticoid receptors to induce transcription of apical ENaC sodium channels and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
Blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
questions.explain: Aldosterone binds cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptors, inducing expression of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), ROMK potassium channels, and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase pumps.

open.q: Name the apical sodium channel upregulated by aldosterone in renal collecting duct principal cells.

questions.q: Why does cortisol not normally overstimulate renal mineralocorticoid receptors despite circulating at 100-fold higher concentrations than aldosterone?
options: Cortisol cannot enter renal tubular cells
Mineralocorticoid receptors have zero affinity for cortisol
Renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol into inactive cortisone
questions.explain: 11-beta-HSD2 in aldosterone-target tissues inactivates cortisol to cortisone; inhibition of this enzyme by glycyrrhetinic acid in black licorice causes apparent mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension and hypokalemia).

open.q: Name the renal enzyme that converts active cortisol into inactive cortisone to protect mineralocorticoid receptors.

questions.q: Which two plasma biomarkers are most specific for diagnosing acute myocardial necrosis following coronary occlusion?
options: Cardiac troponin I and cardiac troponin T
questions.explain: Cardiac-specific troponins I and T (cTnI and cTnT) are structural regulatory proteins of the cardiomyocyte thin filament that rise within 3-6 hours of myocardial infarction and remain elevated for 7-10 days.

open.q: Name the two cardiac-specific regulatory proteins measured in serum as the gold-standard biomarkers of myocardial infarction.
accept: Cardiac troponin I and troponin T

questions.q: Which peptide hormone is released by ventricular cardiomyocytes in response to volume overload and myocardial wall stretch, serving as a diagnostic biomarker for heart failure?
questions.explain: B-type (brain) natriuretic peptide (BNP) and NT-proBNP are secreted by ventricular myocardium under stretch, promoting natriuresis, diuresis, and vasodilation via cGMP.

open.q: Name the natriuretic peptide secreted by ventricular myocardium in response to wall stretch that is used to diagnose heart failure.

questions.q: Which peptide hormone secreted predominantly by the gastric fundus rises before meals to stimulate appetite via hypothalamic NPY/AgRP neurons?
questions.explain: Ghrelin is an orexigenic hormone secreted by gastric X/A-like cells during fasting that stimulates hypothalamic neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons as well as growth hormone release.

open.q: Name the orexigenic hormone secreted by the stomach during fasting to stimulate hunger.

questions.q: Why is the ocular lens particularly susceptible to osmotic cataract formation during chronic hyperglycemia in diabetes mellitus?
options: Insulin directly precipitates lens crystallin proteins
Glucose is converted to uric acid inside the lens
Aldose reductase converts excess glucose to sorbitol, which accumulates and draws water into lens fibres
questions.explain: Insulin-independent glucose entry into the lens saturates hexokinase, shunting glucose through aldose reductase to sorbitol; low lens sorbitol dehydrogenase traps sorbitol, drawing water inward and opacifying lens fibers.

open.q: Name the sugar alcohol that accumulates in the ocular lens during hyperglycemia to cause osmotic cataract formation.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation of L-DOPA to dopamine in dopaminergic and noradrenergic neurons?
questions.explain: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (DOPA decarboxylase) requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) to convert L-DOPA to dopamine (and 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin).

open.q: Name the pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme that converts L-DOPA to dopamine.

questions.q: Selective inhibition of monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) by selegiline or rasagiline is useful in Parkinson disease because MAO-B preferentially degrades which neurotransmitter in the striatum?
questions.explain: MAO-A preferentially oxidizes serotonin and norepinephrine, whereas MAO-B selectively deaminates dopamine in the human brain; inhibiting MAO-B preserves striatal dopamine without triggering the tyramine cheese reaction at standard doses.

open.q: Which monoamine neurotransmitter is preferentially degraded by monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) in the striatum?

questions.q: A 45-year-old man taking phenelzine (a non-selective MAO inhibitor) for refractory depression eats aged cheese and cured meats, then develops a severe hypertensive crisis. Which vasoactive amine escaped first-pass degradation?
questions.explain: Tyramine in fermented foods is normally degraded by intestinal and hepatic MAO-A; when MAO is inhibited, tyramine enters sympathetic nerve terminals and displaces large stores of norepinephrine.

open.q: Name the dietary vasoactive amine in aged cheese that precipitates hypertensive crisis in patients taking MAO inhibitors.

questions.q: How do benzodiazepines and barbiturates enhance inhibitory neurotransmission at the GABA-A receptor?
options: Act as competitive antagonists at glycine receptors
Bind allosteric sites on the GABA-A chloride channel to increase chloride influx and hyperpolarize neurons
questions.explain: GABA-A receptors are ligand-gated Cl- channels; benzodiazepines increase the frequency of channel opening in the presence of GABA, whereas barbiturates increase the duration of channel opening.

open.q: Which ion flows into neurons through the GABA-A receptor channel to produce hyperpolarization?

questions.q: Why does glycine act as a major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem, and how does strychnine poisoning cause fatal muscle spasms?
options: Glycine opens postsynaptic Cl- channels, and strychnine competitively blocks glycine receptors
Glycine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, and strychnine activates it
Glycine blocks voltage-gated calcium channels, and strychnine opens them
Glycine stimulates dopamine release, and strychnine depletes it
questions.explain: Glycine binds strychnine-sensitive glycine receptors (Cl- channels) on spinal motor neurons to mediate recurrent inhibition; strychnine blocks these receptors, causing unopposed motor neuron firing and tetanic convulsions.

open.q: Name the inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitter of the spinal cord whose postsynaptic chloride channel receptors are antagonized by strychnine.

questions.q: Why are neurons especially vulnerable to hypoxic-ischemic injury within minutes of cerebral blood flow cessation?
options: Neurons store excess glycogen that is converted to toxic ethanol
High ATP demand and limited energy reserves make neurons vulnerable to pump failure and glutamate-mediated calcium injury
The blood-brain barrier dissolves immediately during hypoxia
Neurons switch exclusively to fatty-acid oxidation during ischaemia
questions.explain: ATP depletion halts Na+/K+-ATPase, depolarizing neurons to release excessive glutamate, which overactivates NMDA receptors and floods cells with Ca2+ that activates proteases, phospholipases, and endonucleases.

open.q: Which ion enters neurons excessively through overactivated NMDA receptors during ischemic glutamate excitotoxicity?

questions.q: Which gaseous retrograde neurotransmitter is synthesized on demand from L-arginine by neuronal nitric oxide synthase and activates soluble guanylyl cyclase without being stored in synaptic vesicles?
questions.explain: Nitric oxide (NO) is a lipid-soluble free radical gas synthesized from arginine by Ca2+/calmodulin-activated nNOS; it diffuses across membranes to activate soluble guanylyl cyclase in target cells.

open.q: Name the gaseous neurotransmitter synthesized from L-arginine that diffuses across membranes to activate soluble guanylyl cyclase.

questions.q: How does botulinum toxin cause flaccid paralysis at the neuromuscular junction?
options: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft
Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels along motor axons
Cleaves SNARE proteins (such as synaptobrevin or SNAP-25) to prevent acetylcholine vesicle fusion and exocytosis
questions.explain: Botulinum toxin is a zinc endopeptidase that cleaves SNARE proteins in presynaptic cholinergic terminals, preventing acetylcholine-containing synaptic vesicles from fusing with the plasma membrane.

open.q: Name the family of vesicle fusion proteins cleaved by botulinum and tetanus toxins to block neurotransmitter exocytosis.

questions.q: How does tetanus toxin produce spastic paralysis rather than flaccid paralysis despite cleaving the same SNARE protein (synaptobrevin) as botulinum toxin?
options: Tetanus toxin travels retrogradely to inhibitory Renshaw interneurons in the spinal cord and blocks GABA and glycine release
Tetanus toxin directly stimulates nicotinic receptors on skeletal muscle
Tetanus toxin increases glutamate synthesis in motor neurons
questions.explain: Tetanus toxin undergoes retrograde axonal transport into the CNS, where it cleaves synaptobrevin in inhibitory spinal interneurons, blocking GABA and glycine release and disinhibiting alpha-motor neurons.

open.q: Which two inhibitory neurotransmitters are prevented from being released in the spinal cord by tetanus toxin?

questions.q: Which protein binds four calcium ions in eukaryotic cells to undergo a conformational change that activates Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinases?
questions.explain: Calmodulin is a ubiquitous EF-hand calcium-binding protein that binds up to four Ca2+ ions and activates downstream enzymes such as CaM kinases, myosin light-chain kinase, and calcineurin.

open.q: Name the ubiquitous intracellular calcium-binding protein that binds four Ca2+ ions to regulate downstream kinases.

questions.q: How do thioamide antithyroid drugs (propylthiouracil and methimazole) reduce thyroid hormone synthesis?
options: Block the sodium-iodide symporter on the basolateral membrane
Destroy thyroid follicular cells via beta radiation
Inhibit thyroid peroxidase-mediated iodide oxidation, organification, and iodotyrosine coupling
Inhibit TSH secretion from the anterior pituitary
questions.explain: Both methimazole and propylthiouracil inhibit thyroid peroxidase (TPO); propylthiouracil additionally inhibits peripheral 5'-deiodinase conversion of T4 to T3.

open.q: Name the key thyroid enzyme inhibited by both methimazole and propylthiouracil.

questions.q: A 46,XY phenotypic female presents with primary amenorrhea, hypertension, and hypokalemia, with absent axillary and pubic hair. Which steroidogenic enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency blocks cortisol and sex steroid synthesis (causing sexual infantilism and phenotypic female genitalia in 46,XY individuals) while shunting pregnenolone/progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone (causing hypertension and hypokalemia).

open.q: Deficiency of which steroidogenic enzyme causes hypertension, hypokalemia, and lack of sex steroid synthesis in both 46,XX and 46,XY individuals?

questions.q: Why does serum unconjugated bilirubin rise markedly during acute massive intravascular or extravascular hemolysis even in a patient with a healthy liver?
options: The rate of heme breakdown exceeds the conjugating capacity of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase
Albumin becomes saturated with conjugated bilirubin
Haptoglobin converts conjugated bilirubin back into unconjugated bilirubin
questions.explain: Hepatic bilirubin conjugation has a finite maximum capacity; accelerated red blood cell destruction overwhelms UGT1A1, causing unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and elevated urinary urobilinogen without bilirubinuria.

open.q: Which form of bilirubin (conjugated or unconjugated) predominates in serum during hemolytic jaundice?

questions.q: Which enzyme in the pulmonary and renal vascular endothelium converts inactive decapeptide angiotensin I into the potent vasoconstrictor octapeptide angiotensin II?
questions.explain: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), a zinc metallopeptidase abundant on pulmonary capillary endothelium, cleaves two C-terminal amino acids from angiotensin I to form angiotensin II and also degrades bradykinin.

open.q: Name the zinc-dependent metallopeptidase that converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II and degrades bradykinin.

questions.q: In photoreceptors in the dark, high intracellular cGMP keeps cation channels open, producing a continuous depolarizing 'dark current' and tonic release of which neurotransmitter?
questions.explain: In darkness, high cGMP maintains open Na+/Ca2+ channels, keeping rods and cones depolarized (~-40 mV) so they continuously release glutamate onto bipolar cells; light hyperpolarizes the photoreceptor and decreases glutamate release.

open.q: Name the neurotransmitter continuously released by retinal rods and cones in the dark.

questions.q: Which enzyme degrades synaptic GABA into succinic semialdehyde, and is inhibited by the antiepileptic drug vigabatrin?
questions.explain: GABA transaminase (GABA-T, a PLP-dependent enzyme) converts GABA and alpha-ketoglutarate into succinic semialdehyde and glutamate; vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA-T to raise brain GABA levels.

open.q: Name the enzyme inhibited by vigabatrin that catabolizes GABA into succinic semialdehyde.

questions.q: A 62-year-old patient with hepatic cirrhosis develops asterixis (flapping tremor), confusion, and stupor after a high-protein meal. Elevated arterial ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier and disrupts neurotransmission primarily by which mechanism?
options: Astrocytic ammonia detoxification raises glutamine, depletes TCA intermediates and causes cellular swelling
Direct activation of dopamine D2 receptors
Inhibition of choline acetyltransferase in the cortex
Excess serotonin synthesis in the brainstem
questions.explain: In hepatic encephalopathy, detoxifying ammonia via glutamine synthetase in astrocytes accumulates osmotically active glutamine (causing cerebral edema) and depletes TCA intermediates and excitatory glutamate pools.

open.q: Which osmotically active amino acid accumulates inside brain astrocytes during hyperammonemic hepatic encephalopathy?

questions.q: What is the biochemical basis of the blood-brain barrier's selective permeability to circulating solutes?
options: Absence of mitochondria in brain capillaries
Tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells restrict paracellular entry; selective transporters carry essential solutes
A thick collagen basement membrane blocks all lipid-soluble molecules
High albumin concentration in CSF forms the main barrier
questions.explain: Tight junctions eliminate paracellular diffusion across brain capillaries; lipophilic molecules (O2, CO2, ethanol, steroid hormones) diffuse freely, while glucose (GLUT1) and large neutral amino acids (LAT1) require specific transporters.

open.q: Name the specialized intercellular junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells that form the physical basis of the blood-brain barrier.
